title: AVIAN FATALITIES at the UMOYA WIND FARM, HOPEFIELD
full_text:
FIRST ANNUAL REPORT ON EFFECTS OF PATTERNED BLADES on AVIAN FATALITIES at the UMOYA WIND FARM, HOPEFIELD
Prepared for: Prepared by: Birds & Bats Unlimited: Environmental Consultants Dr R.E. Simmons / M. Martins

1 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
The Umoya Energy Wind Farm at Hopefield is the first renewable energy project in the southern hemisphere to trial patterned blades to determine if they reduce avian impacts. This report represents the first 12-months’ monitoring of avian fatalities at the (4) patterned blades painted with two broad Signal Red stripes in relation to (16) un-patterned control turbines close by. From nine turbines with high fatality rates, four turbines (T28, T31, T34, T35) were chosen for blade-patterning, each with a nearest neighbour control.
The Umoya carcass searching team completed 12-months of post-treatment surveys from April 2023 to April 2024 and recorded, mainly, Bokmakierie and Cape Spurfowl, but also pigeons, korhaans, Black shouldered Kites and a Peregrine Falcon as bird-strike victims. Their results were compared with two pre-treatment years of monitoring using identical methods to determine pre-patterning fatality rates.
With tower impacts (of Cape Spurfowl and Dikkop) removed, the 12 months’ of post-treatment monitoring revealed a total of 10 fatalities at the total 20 turbines: 0 at the (4) patterned blades and 10 at the (16) controls. The expected number of fatalities after the painting, based on the fatality rates before painting revealed that the four patterned turbines had fewer fatalities (0) than expected (6.5) – indicating a 100% reduction in fatalities for all bird species. This cannot be explained as an overall decrease in fatalities since the un-patterned control turbines had similar numbers of fatalities in the same experimental period (10) as expected (12.0).
Statistical tests comparing observed vs expected fatalities – before and after treatment – for the patterned vs all (16) un-patterned controls were Significant at the p = 0.027 level. Higher significance (p = 0.007) was found when the patterned turbines were comparted with the (4) nearest neighbours. No raptors were killed at the patterned blades after treatment, despite six species accounting for seven fatalities prior to treatment.
These results were not affected by omitting species (e.g. spurfowl) believed to be killed by flying into the towers. The inclusion of all (20) Spurfowl and a Dikkop carcass found as fatalities at the tower bases did not change the significance of patterned blades vs all (16) controls (p = 0.038), or the patterned vs nearest neighbours (p<0.009).
Thus, results at the Umoya Wind Farm indicate that patterning the blades significantly reduces the number of avian fatalities. That it did so after just 12 months, and by 100% for all species, was unexpectedly efficient. While these are small samples, they exceed those achieved with a solid black design in Norway (May et al. 2020: 72%) and are more significant than the unpublished Dutch study (Klop et al. 2024), also with a solid black design.
Further fatality data through 2024 and 2025 will increase the sample sizes and confidence of these first Umoya results and allow a robust assessment over two years. The positive outcome of this study should give confidence to the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) to permit other wind facilities in South Africa, to implement and test this mitigation in areas of high avian diversity.
Based on comparison with other experiments BBU recommends that patterned rather than solid designs may give the best results for reducing avian fatalities.

2 INTRODUCTION
Renewable energy in the form of wind and solar farms provides sustainable green energy with minimal greenhouse gases in a rapidly warming world. Despite these considerable benefits there are environmental costs in terms of species of birds and bats killed by spinning blades and grid connections.
In South Africa, turbines kill on average 4.4 + 2.9 birds per year, or 2.0 + 1.3 birds per MW per year (Perold et al. 2020). And unlike other countries a high diversity of species are killed covering 130 species from 46 families ranging from the smallest waxbills to the largest Martial Eagles (Perold et al. 2020, Simmons and Martins 2024). This review also revealed that the most vulnerable group were raptors (hawks, harriers, eagles, owls) comprising over a third (36%) of the 848 carcasses recovered (Perold et al. 2020). This is in line with other reports of a high toll of raptors elsewhere in South Africa and globally (Simmons and Martins 2019, Thaxter et al. 2017).
Many methods of mitigation have been mooted to reduce this environmental cost – among these is patterning the blades to increase their visibility to passing raptors (May et al. 2020). This is potentially the least financially costly relative to other automated shut down on demand (SDOD) methods.
The Umoya Wind Farm (UWF) in Hopefield is the first to trial this form of mitigation in Africa at the recommendation of Birds & Bats Unlimited (BBU). Umoya successfully convinced the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) to allow patterned blades, but CAA dis-allowed black paint to be used (as in the Norway experiment). Instead, they permitted “Signal Red” as their legislation already allowed this on tall communication towers.
Thus, one blade of four turbines was painted with two broad red stripes as recommended by McIsaac (2001), in early 2023. BBU recommended that turbines with the highest fatality records were treated and that their nearest neighbours and 12 others be used as two sets of controls.
The outcome of this first experiment for the African continent is important not only for the UWF but for other developers in South Africa, as it allows insights into the efficacy of such mitigations. Permitting from CAA has now become easier given that in November 2023 the South African Wind Energy Association (SAWEA) successfully motivated (Morkel et al. 2023) to the CAA for a blanket permit allowing all wind farms the opportunity for patterning their blades.
This “Alternative Means of Compliance” (AMOC) was granted by the SA CAA on 18 January 2024 SAWEA Exemption Outcome letter V1.pdf allowing the South African wind industry the opportunity to pattern their blades. The Umoya example is leading the way in the first field test in Africa and the southern hemisphere.
This first annual report assesses the first 12 months’ of carcass monitoring from April 2023 to April 2024 for the operational Umoya Wind Farm in Hopefield.
Here we compare:
• the fatalities for the (4) patterned turbines before and after patterning with Signal Red, with • the fatalities for the (16) un-patterned (Control) turbines in the same before-after periods. • We also compared fatalities with the (4) nearest neighbour (Control) turbines. • Avian fatalities from 12 months in 2014-2015 (Arcus Consulting 2016) and 12 months in 2020-
2021 (BBU 2021) were used as the controls before any patterning took place.

Our aims here are to understand the effects of patterning the four Umoya turbines in terms of:
(i) any reduction in fatalities at the (4) patterned vs their (4) un-patterned nearest neighbours, (ii) fatalities at the (4) patterned blades vs (16) un-patterned blades before and after treatment,
and (iii) determining if patterning at some turbines increases the collision rate at the neighbouring (un-
patterned) turbines.
Our a-priori prediction is that the number of fatalities will decrease at the patterned turbines (but not the controls) because all birds – and particularly raptors – are more likely to see and avoid the higher contrast blades.
2.1 Background to the Umoya Wind Farm
• The Umoya Wind Farm comprises 37 Vestas 1.8 MW wind turbines with a capacity of 66.6 MW. • It is situated 5-km south-east of Hopefield, straddling the R45 in the Saldanha Bay Municipality,
Western Cape. • Umoya Energy owns three adjoining farms with a combined area of approximately 2400
hectares. Roughly half of this land was designated as a Conservation Area managed by SANParks and will be declared part of the West Coast National Park. • Umoya Energy Wind Farm received Environmental Authorisation in September 2009. • Construction of the wind farm commenced in December 2012. • Commercial production of energy for the South African grid commenced in February 2014.
Because it was felt that threatened Red Data species may be at risk on this farm the Department of Environment (now Department of Forestry, Fisheries and Environment, DFFE) requested that further avian monitoring be undertaken to check this possibility. This has been achieved (Arcus 2016, BBU 2021) and the present carcass searching has been underway since April 2023.
The patterning of the blades took place in situ from January to March 2023 and carcass searching began in mid-April 2023, covering 20 turbines, inclusive of the four patterned blades, weekly to twice monthly.

3 METHODS
The carcass survey methods employed by Arcus in 2014-2015 at the Umoya Wind Facility (UWF) were repeated for the Hopefield carcass search teams in 2020/2021. They used four Environment Survey Assistants (ESAs), working in two pairs at different turbines, and searched for bird and bat carcasses at all 37 turbines at the WEF site from 15 December 2014 to 15 December 2015. This was repeated for 20 turbines in the present 12-months of monitoring. The turbines surveyed were reduced to allow carcass searchers to concentrate their efforts on the (4) patterned turbines and their (16) immediate neighbours. Arcus created search plots with an 80-m radius from each turbine base, in which the ESAs searched for bird and bat carcasses. Circular transects were walked slowly by each pair of ESAs, who remained approximately six metres apart.
The search interval (i.e., the number of days between searches at individual turbines) was seven days. A search schedule for the entire year was created such that the turbines were searched weekly and each turbine covered an equal number of times per year. In total, the number of searches per turbine ranged from 46 to 55, totalling 1866 searches, with differences resulting from logistical reasons, for example holidays, torrential rain, or turbine maintenance. On two occasions when a control turbine (T26) was offline, an adjacent turbine (T27) was employed as the control for the duration (70 days: June - August 2023 and 15 days: November - December 2023). On one occasion the patterned turbine T28 was offline for a week (16-23 August), but no similarly treated turbine could be used in its place.
Each observer was instructed to look for any evidence of possible bird or bat fatalities (regardless of the possible cause of the fatality). They were also instructed to complete fatality reports for any carcasses found outside of the regular search schedule – for example by the onsite staff (including maintenance and security staff) – or while the ESAs travelled around the WEF. All evidence was collected and stored onsite in a freezer and examined by the Bird Specialist to determine the species involved and the most likely cause of death. In the current 12-months monitoring period (April 2023 to April 2024) all carcasses were photographed in situ with a photograph of the GPS coordinates and the closest turbine. These were identified as far as possible by RE Simmons, and extra information was sometimes requested.

Given that biases in the form of carcass removal by scavengers and observers over-looking carcasses can occur, Arcus also set up trials to determine the biases from both sources. This was not repeated in 2020-2021 or in the year under review since site visits were not part of the Terms of Reference.
Large numbers of Cape Spurfowl were found in these pre-treatment surveys, and Arcus (2016) suspected that these birds were hitting the towers and not being killed by the blades. The ESAs in this (2023/24) phase also suspected tower collisions, as many of these birds were found within a few metres of the towers.
Given that the experiments are focused on the ability of birds to avoid high visibility blades and not the towers, all the Spurfowls, and one Dikkop also found next to the tower (with an impact mark on the tower) were removed from the analysis. This removed 12 (of 50) individual birds from the “Before” group, and 8 (of 18) from the “After” group. This reduced the sample size and, thus, the power of the tests but was felt to be more biologically accurate.
Similar observations for fast-flying, low-agility game birds were made in Norway where Willow Ptarmigan Lagopus lagopus collide with towers (Stokke et al. 2020), and this has also been reported in Spain (F Cervantes pers comm). The tower-strikes were also removed from their analyses.
3.1 Study area and experimental design
The UWF turbines chosen for patterning were from those exhibiting either:
(i) the highest overall fatalities based on the previous sampling; or (ii) fatalities to Red Data species.
Of the nine turbines that fell within these parameters, four were chosen for treatment: T28, T31, T34, T35 (see Table 1 for details). The locations of these are shown in Figure 1. For each treated turbine its nearest neighbour was chosen as a (unpainted) control turbine. An additional 12 un-patterned turbines were also used as controls for other analyses. All of these turbines fell in a “high impact” zone in the northern section of the UWF.
The study area lies within the Fynbos biome, in Endangered Hopefield Sand Fynbos (Mucina and Rutherford 2011). Vegetation is intact but previously farmed throughout the farm. It lies in a winter rainfall area with a mean annual precipitation of 326-mm and mean maximum temperature of 28.3o C and minimum of 7.1o C. Misty days are common in winter (Mucina and Rutherford 2011). Daylight hours for Cape Town range from 14.25 hours at the height of summer to 9.54 hours in winter (Sunrise and sunset in Cape Town (timeanddate.no)
3.2 Statistical tests
Note that the Chi-square (X2) test statistic used here to test for significant differences is given for indicative purposes only because it does not handle small numbers (such as zeros) very well. Each test was repeated with the Barnard’s Unconditional Test that is more appropriate for small samples. The results were identical to the X2 tests, so we have retained the X2 test results here. Once future fatalities are sampled under the patterned and control turbines then more sophisticated statistical tests (Generalized Linear Models [GLMs]) will be undertaken by Dr F Cervantes. Initial tests, done to date largely support the less sophisticated tests here.

The identification of “problem” turbines was used to choose where the patterned blade mitigation would best be focussed for conservation purposes. Overall, they were responsible for 50% of the 75 known avian fatalities over 24 months. The four turbines chosen for patterning were responsible for 25% of all 75 fatalities (n=19), with spurfowl included. These turbines were T28, T31, T34, and T35 and were each responsible for three or more fatalities. This included a total of seven raptor fatalities and notably an Endangered Black Harrier, prior to treatment. With spurfowl removed, fatalities for most turbines was reduced to three birds, with a maximum of four fatalities at T35. The nine turbines were then responsible for 47% of 55 deaths.
Because avian fatality rates were recorded before and after patterning, we can use the powerful BACI test (where B = Before, A = After, C = Control, I = Impact) to statistically test the effect of experimentally patterning the “Impact” turbines on fatalities before and after treatment. 4.2 Avian fatalities at the Patterned turbines vs all Control turbines
During the present 12 months monitoring a total of 18 avian fatalities were recorded: 16 at the unpatterned turbines, and two at the patterned turbines (Table 3, Appendix 1). Eight of the 18 were spurfowl or dikkops, presumed to be tower deaths, and were removed from further analysis. Thus, 10 fatalities were recorded, all at the control turbines and none at the patterned turbines. We can interpret this result by calculating the number of fatalities that were expected.

Given that the previous rates of fatality were:
• 24 birds in 24 months at the 16 control turbines (= 0.063 fatalities/turbine/month) and • 13 birds in 24 months at the 4 turbines to be patterned (= 0.135 fatalities/turbine/month) then,
over 12 months we expect:
• at the 16 control turbines (16*12*0.063 =) 12.0 fatalities and • at the 4 patterned turbines (4*12*0.135 =) 6.5 fatalities.
However, as shown in Table 3, the number of fatalities recorded at the patterned blades in 12 months was 0 (zero) birds, not 6.5 birds. The number of fatalities recorded at the (16) control turbines, however, was similar to that expected (10 vs 12.0).
Thus, it appears that the number of deaths occurring at the patterned blades showed a 100% reduction – (0 vs 6.5), and this was not due to a general decrease in overall fatalities.
Note too that raptors were not absent from the Umoya Wind Farm (which might explain the low fatality rates). This was borne out by the loss of two Black shouldered Kites and a Peregrine Falcon at the 16 Control turbines in the 12 months under review (Appendix 1). Other species killed were Cape Spurfowls (removed from the analysis), Southern Black Korhaan, Bokmakierie, canaries, pigeons and a Little Grebe.
Observations of live birds at the farm in September/October 2023 by RES and bird specialist Eric Herrmann also recorded five raptor species present and active on the farm including: Jackal Buzzard (x2) breeding, Yellow-billed Kite (x4), Black-shouldered Kite (x3) breeding, Rock Kestrel x2 and Black Harrier (x1).
All were recorded around the north-western section of the farm, where the patterned blades are being trialled and this suggests these species were avoiding turbines that had previously proven fatal.

4.4 Do birds seeing the patterned blades divert into the nearest neighbours?
A potentially confounding issue of patterning blades is that once birds see them, they could veer away and into nearby turbines, increasing the fatality rate at the nearest neighbours. This possibility was checked by comparing fatality rates of the nearest neighbours (NN) before and after patterning, with the other (12) controls before and after patterning. There was no significant effect (Figure 4). In other words, there was no increase in the number of fatalities at the nearest neighbours of the experimental turbines, relative to the other controls. This potential side effect does not appear to be an issue at the Umoya Wind Farm, and it was, likewise, not an effect at the Smøla wind farm in Norway (May et al. 2020).

4.5 The role of towers in avian deaths
This analysis of fatalities at the Umoya Wind Farm focussed on birds being killed by the turbine blades. However, some birds appear to be killed by impacting the towers, especially Cape Spurfowl. This was first recognised by the Arcus carcass search teams (Arcus 2016) and has been suspected by the Umoya ESAs in the season under review. Many spurfowl carcasses are found within a few metres of the tower and their heavy wing loading in combination with their dawn and dusk flights, in small flocks, suggest they don’t see the white towers and impact them. One Spotted Dikkop, a known nocturnal species, was also found less than 2-m from a tower and an impact mark about 8-m high was found on the tower (N Mackay pers comm). All of these birds were removed from analysis reported here, as the experiment was designed to test increased visibility of the blades, not the towers.
The question becomes: what is the effect on the statistical power if they are not removed? That is, if all the birds presumed to be killed by the towers are retained in the analyses. We re-analysed all comparisons with all spurfowl and dikkops included (n = 20 birds) and found that the effect of patterned turbines on fatalities had no influence on the results (Table 5).

The inclusion of presumed tower victims made no difference in comparisons of the (4) nearest neighbour with the patterned blades, nor was the Significance affected for the comparisons with all (16) controls and patterned blades. Comparing controls with controls (to answer the question do birds veer away from the patterned blades into the nearest neighbours) we also find no effect including or excluding spurfowl (Table 5). The only change was a reduction in fatalities at the patterned blades where two tower victims (a Cape Spurfowl and a Spotted Dikkop) decreased the effect from a 100% drop in fatalities to 80%. For raptors, the decrease in fatalities remained at 100% (7 victims to 0 victims). Thus, the results are robust with or without the inclusion of presumed tower fatalities.
In summary, the patterning of four turbine blades resulted in significant reductions in fatalities whether they are compared with all other unpainted (control) turbines or compared with just their four nearest neighbouring controls. Given that 6.5 fatalities were expected (based on pre-treatment fatality rates) at the patterned blades in the 12 months’ following patterning, and none were recorded, the patterning of blades appears to make blades more visible to all birds.
Furthermore, there were no more raptors killed, post-treatment, despite seven individuals of six raptors species being killed by the blades pre-treatment. Thus, the patterning also seems to be effective for the most highly collision-prone species – raptors. These samples are small and represent only 12 months of monitoring by the Umoya team, but they are, nevertheless, hugely promising results. A further 12 months’ will increase confidence in understanding their long-term efficacy.
5 COSTS AND COMMERCIAL CONSIDERATIONS

5.1 Cost of Works
The works required the provision of a specialist platform, suspended from the nacelle of the wind turbine, to provide safe access for the technicians to carry out the works. The total cost of the provision of specialist equipment, crane hire, specialist labour, materials and general consumables amounted to a total cost of R 2.46m for the 4 turbines.
5.2 Impact on electricity production
Every effort was taken to conduct the required works during periods of low wind, thereby minimising the impact on electricity production, but this has to be considered against the costs of having hired

equipment (most specifically the platform) standing idle while incurring ongoing hire costs. In total the time required to take each of the 4 turbines out of service to complete the works resulted in a total loss of generation revenue of R 328 000.
5.3 Warranty and commercial considerations
In this specific instance Vestas, the Original Equipment Supplier and Operator of the wind turbines, agreed to maintain the exact same warranty terms for the patterned turbines. That said, the risk of major component failure lies with the project owners. The weight of the two coats of paint applied to each blade totalled 26.4 kg and both Vestas and the Management team will continue to monitor the performance of the painted turbines to establish whether or not there is any noticeable impact on the wear of critical components of these turbines as a result of this additional weight being applied to a single blade.
5.4 Future cost considerations
Umoya note that the cost of retrospectively painting wind turbine blades is significant (in the case of Umoya R607 000 per turbine), especially for wind farms with a large number of wind turbines. However, where patterned blades are ordered as part of the supply of new wind turbines to new projects, the cost of such work in-factory is negligible, if any.
6 CONCLUSIONS
The operational Umoya Wind Farm at Hopefield is the first such farm in the southern hemisphere, or Africa, to experiment with patterning their turbine blades to reduce avian impacts. Single blades at four turbines were painted with two broad Signal Red stripes (as recommended by McIsaac 2001) early in 2023 to determine the subsequent effect on avian fatality rates at these turbines. The Umoya carcass searching team completed the first 12-months of carcass surveys from April 2023 to April 2024.
Their results were compared with two previous years’ monitoring using identical methods and found: • Most of the present-day fatalities were Bokmakieries and Cape Spurfowl, but included two raptor species – Peregrine Falcon and Black shouldered Kites, as well as korhaans, grebes, doves, and canary; • The spurfowl were removed from further analysis because they may be chiefly tower collision victims; • The four turbines given a patterned blade were T28, T31, T34, T35 as these turbines previously showing high fatality rates (with spurfowl). These were compared with 16 un-patterned controls as well as their four nearest neighbours. • In the 12-months since the experiment began, no fatalities were recorded at the four patterned turbines. Elsewhere, 10 fatalities were recorded at the white control turbines. • Did patterning lead to fewer fatalities? The expected number of fatalities at the patterned turbines after treatment, based on their fatality rates before treatment (13 in 24 months) indicate that they had fewer fatalities after 12 months (0 birds) than expected (6.5 birds). • This was not due to a general decrease in fatalities because the un-patterned turbines had similar numbers of fatalities (10) as that expected (12.0).

• A simple X2 statistical test of the observed vs expected fatalities for (4) patterned vs all (16) control turbines indicates a significant difference before and after (p = 0.027).
• A second X2 test of the observed vs expected fatalities for the patterned turbines vs their (4) nearest neighbours showed an even more significant result (p < 0.007). That is, the result is unlikely to be due by chance alone.
• To check if removing tower-victims made any difference to the results, we added all 20 victims back to the analysis and found no difference in the significance values for all comparisons.
• All statistical tests were repeated with Barnard’s Unconditional test and found to give identical probabilities as the X2 tests.
• The costs of retrospectively painting blades on the Umoya wind farm was significant, but the cost of doing so on new projects is likely to be minimal, if any.
We conclude that the initial results of the first 12 months’ of monitoring of the four patterned and 16 surrounding white turbines are very promising as they show a 100% reduction in (unadjusted) fatalities for the patterned blades, relative to that expected from previous fatalities at the same turbines.
That this occurred over a period of just 12 months was unexpectedly efficient and suggests other wind farms would benefit from this simple mitigation measure. The samples are still low given the low fatality rate at the Umoya farm and, thus, the experiment should continue for a further 12 months.
6.1 Comparisons with other studies
It is worth noting that the results obtained from this Africa-first experiment have achieved higher reductions in avian fatalities (100%) than the only other published experiment with a black blade mitigation in Norway where a 71.9% reduction in fatalities was achieved for all bird species (May et al. 2020). It also gives significant results that were not achieved in the Dutch black-blade experiments (with seven turbines and their neighbouring controls) on the coast at Eemshaven after 12 months (Klop et al. 2024).
The Norwegian study however, found a remarkable (100%) reduction in eagle deaths at the four blackpainted turbines after 10 years, with the unpainted turbines continuing to kill eagles at a rate of six per year (Stokke et al. 2024). We achieved similar results but with much smaller samples: seven raptors of six species were killed at the four patterned turbines prior to painting at Umoya (Black Harrier, Booted Eagle, Buzzard spp, Rock Kestrel, Jackal Buzzard x2, Barn Owl) but since patterning no raptors have been killed in 12 months.
Thus, both experiments indicate that the most frequently killed suite of birds –raptors – avoid turbine blades made more visible with black or red paint.
A Spanish study underway at Navarre with black blades, run by Iberdrola, has yet to publish its findings, which may suggest it, too, is not achieving similarly clear-cut results. We suggest that the rapid success achieved at Umoya could be due to the use of a patterning design (two broad stripes) rather than a solid black design. It is unlikely to arise from the use of red rather than black paint as the high contrast achieved by black and white is known to be the best colour combination visible to raptors (Potier et al 2018, Martin and Banks 2023).

As such, we suggest that patterns (two stripes) rather than a solid design in signal red or black may be the best option to increase visibility. We must await further results from these and other field experiments before any firm conclusions can be reached.

by SETA CAROL AGHABABIAN B.S. California Lutheran University, 2020 University of Colorado Colorado Springs A thesis submitted to the Graduate Faculty of the University of Colorado Colorado Springs in partial fulfillment of the

Aghababian, Seta Carol (M.S., Biology)

Bat Behavior at Commercial Wind Turbines as Revealed by 3-D Thermal Videography Thesis Directed by Assistant Professor Aaron J. Corcoran.

## **ABSTRACT**

The wind industry is rapidly growing, yet lethal interactions between bats and industrial-scale wind turbines remain an ecological drawback of this valuable renewable energy source. Previous research has utilized two-dimensional video to describe bat

behavior, however it is unable to provide quantifiable spatial metrics that may be important in determining why collisions occur and inform development of collision minimization systems. Our study represents the first utility-scale application of threedimensional video, a method capable of accurately measuring the position of animals in space, used to measure bat activity patterns at commercial wind turbines. We reconstructed 22,479 flight paths of nocturnal aerial animals across 89 recording nights at two wind turbines in a utility-scale wind energy facility in Iowa, USA between August and October of 2021. We observed 68% of vertebrate animal flights at heights within the rotor-swept zone where they are at danger of colliding with blades. Activity was 300% higher in the lower half of the rotor-swept zone (below the turbine nacelle) compared to the upper half. We found that activity within and above the rotor swept area is concentrated during a small range of dates in late August, early evening hours, and for winds blowing to the south between 3 and 6 meters per second, supporting the theory that bat mortality is related to peaks in migration activity. For a subset of 23 nights distributed across the sampling period, we manually classified the behavior of 4,252 flight paths. Linear flight behaviors were more common above the turbine, whereas non-linear behaviors were more common at altitudes in the lower rotor-swept zone. We also

reconstructed two collisions with the turbine which suggests that wind turbulence may be

a proximate cause of collision. Our findings indicate that while three-dimensional video may not be necessary for general activity studies, it will be valuable in understanding how best to deploy targeted minimization systems, such as acoustic deterrents, and

provide in-depth characterizations of bat behavior near turbines that will help elucidate the underlying cause of collisions.

## **INTRODUCTION**

Energy crises in the late 20[th] century, namely the oil embargo of 1973, highlighted a global need to diversify energy resources beyond fossil fuels (Mittlefehldt, 2018).

Countries recognized renewable energy sources as reliable alternatives and more recently as viable options to mitigate climate change (Luderer et al., 2014). Consequently,

renewable energy industries, such as solar, wind, and biofuel, grew rapidly over the last several decades and renewable energy production now accounts for about one quarter of global power generation (IRENA, 2022; REN21, 2022). Wind is favored as a renewable energy source because it is possible to generate electricity using wind turbines in most countries, turbines do not emit greenhouse gas during electricity production, and energy production costs are competitive with other renewables like solar (Jaber, 2014; REN21, 2022). Globally, nearly $1.3 trillion USD was spent to develop wind energy over the last decade, and wind energy production has increased exponentially since 2000 in regions like Europe, North America, and Asia (IRENA & CPI, 2023; Kaldellis & Zafirakis, 2011). Currently, China, the United States, and Germany are the leading wind energy producers, however, the industry is expected to grow globally as other countries, such as Brazil and India, are making large investments towards developing wind energy facilities (REN21, 2022).

While wind energy is economically beneficial to global energy generation and contributes to countering climate change, there is evidence that wind turbines negatively affect wildlife, especially flying animals that collide with turbines. Video surveys have

recorded birds (Aschwanden et al., 2015; McClure et al., 2021) and bats (Cryan et al. 2014; Horn et al., 2008) flying near turbine structural components and carcasses collected below wind turbines exhibit injuries (e.g. lacerations, fractures, limb amputations)

consistent with contacting turbines during flight (Baerwald et al., 2008; Ferri et al.,

2011). Animals can collide with stationary turbine structures, such as the monopole, but collisions primarily occur in the rotor swept zone (RSZ; Figure 1) where the rotor blades strike an animal in flight (Choi et al., 2020). Research focused on addressing bird

fatalities has resulted in simple interventions that could reduce fatalities and do not affect energy production, such as aviation lighting (Gehring et al., 2009). However, reducing bat fatalities has been a challenge despite considerable effort. There is no consensus as to why bats are attracted to wind turbines (Guest et al., 2022) and the only proven mitigation method, curtailment (turning turbines off at low wind speeds when they produce relatively little energy), reduces energy production. Figure 1. The anatomy of a large wind turbine (art by Maddison Simmons and Gail Shultz).

Australian wildlife surveys recorded the first evidence of bat fatalities caused by turbine collisions (Hall and Richards, 1972; Tate, 1952). Since then, bat turbine fatalities are recognized as a global issue with carcasses observed at wind facilities across North America (Davy et al., 2020; Erickson and Gritski, 2003; Kerns and Kerlinger, 2004; Brown and Hamilton, 2006a; Jain et al., 2011), South America (Barros et al., 2015; Escobar et al., 2015), Europe (Camina, 2012; Georgiakakis et al., 2012; Lehnert et al. 2014; Măntoiu et al., 2020; Marques et al., 2018), Africa (Doty and Martin, 2013) and Asia (Chou et al., 2017; Kumar et al., 2013). In well-studied regions, such as North America and Europe, it is currently estimated that hundreds of thousands of bats die each year from colliding with turbines, with millions likely dying over the last two decades (Voigt et al., 2022). Furthermore, the rapid expansion of wind energy with newer technology, such as taller turbines and larger rotor swept zones (Wiser et al., 2022), that pose greater risk to bats (Barclay et al., 2007) suggest the problem is only expected to worsen. Wind energy development can cause large bat population declines, sometimes as much as 91%, during a short period of only a few years (Davy et al., 2021). Across a longer range, effects can become dire with certain species risking extinction in the next 50 to 100 years (Frick et al., 2017; Friedenberg and Frick., 2021). Loss of these species could have far-reaching environmental and economic effects. For example, species affected by turbines perform valuable environmental services, such as pest control (Fill et al., 2022), likely worth billions of dollars to agricultural industries (Boyles et al., 2011; Maine and Boyles, 2015). Therefore, it is important to address turbine fatalities to prevent bat population decline and global economic and environmental losses.

Technological solutions such as acoustic deterrents and turbine curtailment algorithms have been proposed as methods to prevent bat turbine fatalities. Bats use ultrasonic echolocation frequencies for spatial orientation, communication, and foraging (Jones and Holderied, 2007). However, some bats avoid ultrasound from external

sources, such as conspecifics (Loeb and Britzke, 2010) and insects (Hristov and Conner, 2005). Acoustic deterrents are devices that broadcast high frequency sounds used by bats and are an active research area to prevent bat fatalities. Deterrents mounted to turbine nacelles can reduce bat fatalities by 21-78%, however deterrent effectiveness varies by species (Arnett et al., 2013; Weaver et al., 2020) and possible increase fatality rates of others (Schirmacher, 2020). Because higher frequencies attenuate more quickly in the air, it is difficult if not impossible to design acoustic deterrents that cover the entire rotorswept area of large turbines at all frequencies used by bats (Arnett et al., 2013). An alternative to acoustic deterrents is curtailment, where rotors are automatically feathered or slowed during conditions associated with high collision risk (e.g., low wind speed). Curtailment is currently the most effective method to reduce bat fatalities (Adams et al., 2021; Whitby et al., 2021; Voigt et al., 2022) and in some instances, turbine curtailment can reduce fatality rates by 33-79% (Whitby et al., 2021). Although energy losses can seem minimal, ranging from 0.6 to 3.2% loss in annual energy production (Whitby et al., 2021), it is important for these systems to be highly optimized to prevent any unnecessary energy production losses accrued during curtailment (Rogers, 2020). Turbine curtailment models are typically developed to find the conditions associated with the highest fatality rates or activity levels at wind turbines (Behr et al., 2017; Barré et al., 2023; Korner-Nievergelt et al., 2013). For fatality prevention systems to be effective, it is

necessary to understand what bat species, flight behaviors, and environmental conditions

are associated with high collision risk.

Bat turbine fatalities vary regionally; however, fatality rates are strongly

associated with species with certain flight patterns and evolutionary strategies. Globally, aerial-hawking bats, or those that capture prey in the open air (Jones and Rydell, 2003), that travel at high altitudes tend to collide with turbines more frequently than other bat species. For example, Davy’s naked-backed bat ( _Pteronotus davyi_ ) in Mexico, common noctules ( _Nyctalus noctule_ ) in Europe, and Hoary bats ( _Lasiurus cinereus_ ) in the United States and Canada (Arnett et al., 2016). However, this trend does not encompass the full scope of species at risk. For instance, a study in Puerto Rico recorded several fatalities among frugivorous phyllostomid bats which tend to fly at low altitudes, like _Artibeus jamaicensis_ (Rodríguez-Durán and Feliciano-Robles, 2015). It is important to highlight that little is known about fatality trends in tropical regions with diverse bat species, like Asia, South America, and Africa (Arnett et al., 2016). This is likely because many countries from these regions have only begun investing heavily in wind energy during the last decade (IRENA, 2022). In temperate areas like Europe and North America, where bat turbine fatalities have been studied more extensively since the late 2000s, fatalities tend to follow global trends with high-flying, aerial-hawking species composing most

fatalities (Arnett et al., 2016). However, these species are also predominantly tree-

roosting migrants (Arnett et al., 2016; EUROBAT, 2023). Migratory bats are

characterized by seasonal movement over long distances, sometimes over 1500km, and several degrees in latitude (Flemming and Eby, 2003). As opposed to more permanent roosting sites in enclosed spaces such as caves, tree bats exhibit ephemeral roosting

behavior and rest in semi-protected sites found in tree cavities or foliage (Kunz and Lumsden, 2003). In Europe, tree-roosting, migratory species, specifically common pipistrelles ( _Pipistrellus pipistrellus_ , 22%), Nathusius’ pipistrelles ( _Pipistrellus nathusii_ , 16%), and common noctules ( _Nyctalus noctule_ , 15%; EUROBAT, 2023) compose about half of all bat turbine fatalities. In North America, the vast majority (78.4%) of recovered carcasses are tree-roosting migratory bats. These species include hoary bats ( _Lasiurus cinereus_ , 38%), eastern red bats ( _Lasiurus borealis_ , 22%), and silver-haired bats

( _Lasionyvteris noctivagans_ , 18.4%; Arnett and Baerwald, 2013). Because fatality rates are especially high for migratory tree bats in the United States, several hypotheses have been proposed to explain why turbine collisions are common among these species (Table 1). However, these hypotheses are not mutually exclusive and may be acting synergistically at varying spatial scales. Collisions could be random if all bats exhibit equal collision risk, however this seems unlikely because risk is biased by age, sex, and species. Juveniles of some species may be at higher risk as they have less flight experience. Population analysis by Kruszynski et al. (2022) concluded that juvenile Nathusius’ pipistrelles are disproportionately killed by wind turbines near forests and bodies of water. Additionally, collision risk is likely related to an individual’s sex, for example female common noctules spend more time near turbines and approach turbines more often than males (Roeleke et al. 2016). Sex-biased risk may also be

species-specific because hoary bat, eastern red bat, and silver-haired bat fatalities are mostly male (Arnett et al. 2008). Lastly, tree bat collisions in North America occur

mostly during the fall migration between August and September, and migratory species constitute the majority of fatalities during this period (Arnett and Baerwald, 2013; Choi et

al., 2020; Fiedler et al., 2007). In contrast, summer-resident species, such as little brown bats ( _Myotis lucifugus_ ) and big brown bats ( _Eptesicus fuscus_ ), maintain regular activity, but constitute only 0-13.5% of turbine fatalities (Arnett et al., 2008). This suggests that other seasonally migratory species are at greater turbine collision risk.

Because turbine fatalities occur mostly in the fall, it is also possible that turbine collisions occur because of migratory behaviors. In the United States, most wind energy facilities are in Texas, Iowa, and Oklahoma (U.S. Energy Information Administration, 2023; Figure 2). These regions are in modelled migratory routes taken by eastern red bats, hoary bats, and silver-haired bats (Wieringa et al., 2021; Figure 3). Therefore, bats may be coincidentally colliding with turbines because wind energy facilities were constructed along their migration routes. Some bat species may also be at increased risk for coincidental collisions because they are naturally active in air space that overlaps with the RSZ. For example, European free-tailed bats ( _Tadarida teniotis_ ) are more likely to fly at heights within a turbine RSZ compared to _Myotis_ sp. which are rarely detected far from the ground (Wellig et al. 2018). Roemer et al. (2020) reconfirmed that flight altitude is correlated to collision risk and high-flying _Tadarida_ species are at higher collision risk than low-flying _Myotis_ species.

title: Mortality at wind-farms is positively related to large-scale distribution and aggregation in griffon vultures
abstract: Wind-farms have negative impacts on the environment, mainly through habitat destruction and bird mortality, making it urgent to design predictive tools to use in landscape planning. A frequent assumption of wind-farm assessment studies is that bird distribution and abundance and bird mortality through collision with turbines are closely related. However, previous results are contradictory and question the usefulness of these variables to select safer wind-farm locations. We focused on a species highly vulnerable to collision at wind-farms, the griffon vulture, to test whether mortality at turbines was related to the relative position of turbines within the vulture population. We used the location of all turbines on 34 wind-farms in southern Spain, details on 342 griffon vultures found dead, and the location and size of breeding colonies and roost sites of the species during the breeding and non-breeding seasons, respectively. Using variables that describe the large-scale distribution and aggregation of vultures, we found that year-round mortality at turbines increased when they were located in highly populated areas, a result that can be translated into management guidelines to plan wind-farm locations.

## 1. Introduction

Wind-farms have received public and governmental support as alternative energy sources that do not contribute to air pollution as associated with fossil fuel technologies (Leddy et al., 1999). However, the expansion of wind power has environmental impacts (i.e., habitat removal, construction of roads and power lines, visual impact; Laiolo and Tella, 2006; Kuvlesky et al., 2007) that need to be evaluated and considered. In this sense, the primary emphasis of the majority of wind farm-wildlife research has been devoted to investigate how wind farm development has impacted bird and bat populations (e.g., Langston and Pullan, 2003; Baerwald et al., 2008; Garvin et al., 2011), in particular collision rates of birds with turbines as well as factors influencing interspecific and local variability (reviewed in Drewitt and Langston (2006,

> ⇑ Corresponding author. Tel.: +34 954 89 00 75.

> E-mail address: mcarrete@upo.es (M. Carrete).

2008), Kuvlesky et al. (2007), and Stewart et al. (2007)). Both aspects are central in decision-making for managers and policy makers dealing with landscape and environmental planning. An important point in the discussion of potential wind-farm effects on wildlife is the idea that collision mortality increases with bird abundance (Musters et al., 1996; Osborn et al., 2000; Drewitt and Langston, 2006; Tellería, 2009a,b). Although linearity in this relationship could be a priori a simplistic assumption because of interspecific differences in susceptibility to this infrastructure, higher abundance of individuals of species sensitive to collision at wind-farms would increase fatality rates. Scientific evidence on this subject is not conclusive, but environmentalists and managers have used this argument as a precautionary measure against the installation of wind-farms in areas with high densities of sensitive birds such as vultures and other large raptors (e.g., Kingsley and Whittam, 2005; Atienza et al., 2008).

Recently, de Lucas et al. (2008) offered a result that challenges this frequent assumption of wind-farm assessment, since bird

abundance and bird mortality through collision with wind turbines were not closely related in their study. Authors surveyed the relative abundance (i.e., the number of birds that crossed turbine rows within 250 m of a turbine, averaged per season and year) of 10 bird species (nine raptors and one stork) during four periods (pre-breeding, breeding, post-breeding, and winter) in 2000–2002 at two wind-farms in Tarifa, southern Spain, to relate bird fatality rates recorded from 1993 to 2003 to these abundances. Among all species studied, the griffon vulture was the species most frequently killed by wind turbine collision, so authors used information on seasonal changes in its abundance and mortality (the larger number of dead birds in winter from 1993 to 2003 vs their higher abundance during winters of 2000–2001 and 2001–2002) to show a lack of relationship between mortality rate and bird abundance. Generalizing their results, authors did not find a correlation between species’ mortality and their abundances at both wind-farms studied. Barrios and Rodríguez (2004), however, found that high abundances of individuals and, in particular, large numbers passing within 5 m of the blades of an operating wind turbine (which the authors considered as a ‘risk situation’) were the main determinants of high mortality rates at the same two wind-farms. Indeed, most dead griffon vultures were found at the wind-farm where the number of vultures observed and the overall risk of passing near turbines was higher (spatial pattern of mortality), and when vultures were more abundant and wind conditions forced them to pass more frequently near turbines (i.e., in winter). Unlike de Lucas et al. (2008), data gathered by Barrios and Rodríguez (2004) on vulture abundances suggested that birds at risk and mortality corresponded to the same study period, thus strengthening their results. However, contradictions between these studies should be resolved in order to correctly guide the installation of future wind-farms in this and other areas also important for bird conservation. Moreover, to increase our ability to estimate expected mortality instead of to simply measure it, it is also important to develop predictive tools to guide landscape planning, and in this way reduce bird mortality at wind-farms. Currently, risk assessment studies performed before wind-farm construction include the distance to different bird nest sites, including colonies of griffon vultures, as a variable to predict the potential risk of a development (Ferrer et al., 2011). However, the final evaluation encompasses all information applied to a subjective assessment, without using any objective, or standardized criteria. The high mortality rates recorded for species such as the griffon vulture at some of these approved wind-farms clearly show that some of these measures have not been well designed.

Here, we tested the key assumption that turbines located in areas with larger abundances of individuals of species sensitive to collision kill more birds than turbines located in areas with lower local abundances of the same species. Distance to colonies can also be a descriptor of mortality (Atienza et al., 2008), although variability in colony size could be important to explain differences in mortality rates among turbines. Thus, our main prediction is that large aggregations of griffon vultures increase probabilities of collision at turbines, resulting in more birds found death at some specific turbines located within high aggregation areas. To test this prediction, we used information on dead griffon vultures gathered from the same area as the previous studies but covering a larger number of wind-farms (34 vs 2), and using precise data on the spatial distribution (i.e., distance between breeding colonies and/or roost sites and turbines) and abundance (measured through an aggregation index, see below) of the species (Fig. 1). Finally, we provide a management criterion to assess potential risk before wind-farm construction using griffon vultures as an example of a species sensitive to these developments.

## 2. Methods

## 2.1. Study area and species

Data used to perform this study were gathered in Campo de Gibraltar and Tarifa, southern Spain (Fig. 1). The area includes a series of mountains up to 840 m above sea level running in a north–south direction. There, turbines of wind-farms are arranged in rows along the ridges of mountains and hills to optimize the harnessing of energy from prevailing east–west winds. The vegetation includes natural open forests of Quercus sp. and shrubs interspersed with agricultural lands used for cattle grazing (for more details, see Barrios and Rodríguez, 2004; de Lucas et al., 2008).

This area is home to many resident species but is also the main European flyway for migratory birds, as well as being an important location for wind-energy production in Europe (by 2010, Cádiz represents ca. 2% of the cumulative installed capacity of the EU; http:// www.ewea.org). Thus, some studies have been carried out to assess wind-farm effects on wildlife by using long-term mortality data taken at the two oldest developments (Barrios and Rodríguez, 2004; de Lucas et al., 2008). The main results of these studies show that most deaths are concentrated in space and time, and include a taxonomic and a migration component (a few species suffered the most losses, with species with resident populations being killed more often than migrating species). Therefore, bird vulnerability at some points at these wind-farms seems to be the resultant of a combination of site-specific (wind-relief interaction at some turbines), species-specific, and seasonal factors.

Our investigation focuses on the species most vulnerable to collision at wind-farms, the griffon vulture. Indeed, more than 50% of all birds found killed at monitored wind-farms during our study period belong to this species (see Supplementary material). Vultures are more likely to collide with turbine blades than many other avian species due to their large size (ca. 10,500 g), and thus reduced manoeuvrability, flight type (i.e., soaring-gliding) and foraging behavior (i.e., search for carcasses in large geographic areas) (Baisner et al., 2010). This long-lived, cliff-nesting scavenger breeds colonially, forming large aggregations of individuals (communal roost) during winter. The global population status of this species has not been quantified accurately, but the species is not believed to approach the thresholds for the population decline criterion of the IUCN Red List. The current status of the species is therefore evaluated as ‘‘Least Concern’’ (BirdLife International, 2011). In the study area, there is an important sedentary breeding population of griffon vultures (more than 1900 pairs censused in 2008) and a minimum of 4000 birds during winter months (Fig. 1; Natural History Society of Cádiz, unpublished results, 2009). Although breeding colonies and the non-breeding population (i.e., all birds during the non-breeding season) have increased in numbers during recent years, their spatial patterns of relative abundance have remained unchanged (Pearson correlation between colony sizes in 1998 and 2008: r = 0.98, 95% CI = 0.96–0.98, n = 112), and aggregations of birds (i.e., breeding colonies or communal roosts) have remained the same since the beginning of the 1980s (Junco and Barcell, 1997; del Moral, 2009; Natural History Society of Cádiz, unpublished results).

## 2.2. Database and explanatory variables

The complete database we are using includes: (1) the exact location (in UTM units) of all turbines (n = 799) at the 34 windfarms in the study area (public information provided by the Environmental Department of the Junta de Andalucía; Supporting information), (2) details on 342 griffon vultures found killed by turbines (i.e., birds with lacerations, wing injuries, head injuries, back injuries and signs of internal injuries which were certainly

Breeding colonies/roost sites are represented with differently sized squares according to number of breeding pairs/individuals. (b) Detail of the area with highest density of windfarms. Turbines are represented with differently sized dots according to mortality.

caused by a collision) between January 1998 and March 2008, and (3) the spatial distribution and size of breeding colonies and roost sites of griffon vultures during the breeding (February–July) and non-breeding (August–January) seasons, respectively (Fig. 1).

Information on dead vultures, provided by the Environmental Department of the Junta de Andalucía, includes the turbines where birds were found killed, such that a minimum mortality value can be assigned to each. As occurs in the study of de Lucas et al. (2008), which used a sub-sample of the database we are using, information on mortality may contain some flaws and constraints such as the lack of standardized intervals for searches of mortalities at turbines at some wind-farms. As carcasses remain in the field for a period of time longer than the time between successive searches (at least twice a week in all wind-farms, see text) we believe that this source of variability does not seriously bias our results. However, to reduce its potential effects, we have included as a fixed factor the existence of an intensive survey protocol associated with wind-farms with preventive vigilance, consisting on an intensive daily survey of the wind-farm to stop particular turbines to avoid collisions of birds flying in their surrounding (in 24 out of the 34 wind-farms surveyed). In an experiment performed by Barrios and Rodríguez (2004) where authors followed the time to disappearance of eight griffon vultures with known dates of death, they found that all these carcasses persisted within the sampling area for several months. These results are in accordance with other ones showing that small birds disappear earlier and at a higher proportion than larger birds (Smallwood, 2007; Ponce et al., 2010). Thus, as other authors working in the same area (e.g., Barrios and

Rodríguez, 2004; de Lucas et al., 2008), we did not correct for carcass removal by predators and scavengers, this effect being negligible when dealing with large species and monitoring windfarms at least twice a week as in our study area.

The distribution and size of all breeding colonies of the species were obtained through simultaneous census (i.e., all colonies counted at the time) performed by experienced local ornithologists during February–March of 1998 and 2008 (del Moral, 2009). All cliffs known to have been occupied by the species as well as potential suitable sites were visited during the mating, incubation and nestling periods to record their occupancy and the number of breeding pairs through standardized protocols usually applied to this species (del Moral, 2009). During January of 2008 and 2009, the non-breeding population was also monitored by counting (at dusk) individuals in all breeding colonies, which in winter are used as communal roosts, and by observing other potentially suitable roosting sites. In 2008, the griffon vulture population of the study area comprised ca. 2000 breeding pairs distributed in 122 colonies (ranging from 1 to 209 breeding pairs). A minimum of 3800 individuals was counted in the winter while roosting in 60 communal roosts (Fig. 1).

To test whether mortality at turbines was related to the relative position of turbines within the griffon vulture population, we obtained a bird aggregation index (Aggregation) for each turbine for the breeding and the non-breeding seasons using information on griffon vulture distribution (location and mean size of the breeding colonies and communal roosts obtained after averaging breeding censuses of 1998 and 2008, and wintering censuses of 2008 and

2009; del Moral, 2009; Natural History Society of Cádiz, unpublished results). This index was calculated following Moilanen and Hanski (1998) as Aggregationi =[P] exp(dij)Aj where d is distance, i is the ith turbine, j is jth breeding colony or roost site (depending on the season), and Aj is the size (in number of breeding pairs or individuals) of the jth breeding colony or roost site, for the breeding and the non-breeding seasons, respectively. This index actually describes connectivity (sensu Moilanen and Hanski, 1998), larger values representing higher spatial aggregations of the species around each turbine. We also included distance to the nearest breeding colony or roost site of the species in models, depending on the season, because of the usefulness of this variable for management purposes. We considered whether bird mortality throughout the year could be predicted with information on the breeding period, using information of turbine distances to the nearest breeding colony and their aggregation in this period. Distance to breeding colonies is a criterion usually incorporated in risk assessment studies to evaluate the suitability of a site for windfarm construction (Ferrer et al., 2011). Several authors have proposed that turbine attributes may increase collision risk (e.g., Barrios and Rodríguez, 2004; de Lucas et al., 2008). Therefore, we also used information on turbine height and altitude above sea levels as potential predictors of mortality in models.

## 2.3. Analytical procedures

We used Generalized Linear Mixed Models (McCullagh and Searle, 2000) to construct predictive models of bird mortality through the year. We constructed a basic model including variables not related to bird distribution but previously linked to mortality at wind-farms, namely: time since monitoring (the accumulative number of birds killed increases with the number of years a wind-farm is monitored), season (more birds are killed in winter), altitude above sea level and height of turbines (turbine characteristics affect bird mortality) (e.g., Barrios and Rodríguez, 2004; de Lucas et al., 2008). Then, we tested whether variables describing bird abundance near turbines (i.e., aggregation of birds at breeding colonies or roost sites and distance to the nearest breeding colony or roost site) improved the statistical power of the basic model. We modelled number of bird deaths per turbine using the logarithmic link function and the Poisson error distribution. A previous study supports that mortality is spatially aggregated at just a few turbines within wind-farms (Barrios and Rodríguez, 2004). Indeed, a preliminary analysis of the database we are using showed that wind-farms killed griffon vultures differentially, with most deaths (52%) occurring at two developments. Moreover, compared with a random pattern of mortality (i.e., equal mortality rates across turbines), observed values of dead birds at turbines were spatially aggregated in both seasons (breeding season: v[2] = 2385.75, p < 0.001, df = 4; non-breeding season: v[2] = 2854.89, p < 0.001, df = 6), with all dead birds found at 89 turbines during the breeding season (ca. 11% of 799 turbines) and 164 turbines during the non-breeding season (ca. 21% of 799 turbines). Thus, we considered turbines as our sampling units, and they were included (nested within wind-farms) as a random term to control for potential, unmeasured differences among them such as topography or location, while also avoiding non-independence in mortality data.

Models were obtained using the GLIMMIX procedure in SAS 9.2 (SAS Institute Inc., 2009), and their relative explanatory power was compared, penalizing for complexity, using differences in AIC scores (lower scores indicated greater statistical support; Burnham and Anderson, 2002; Richards, 2005). Models with AIC scores differing from that of the lowest score by more than two (i.e., DAIC) were considered to be unsupported statistically (Richards, 2005).

## 3. Results

## 3.1. Distribution, aggregation and mortality of griffon vultures at turbines

The inclusion of a variable describing bird aggregation during the breeding season greatly improved the statistical power of the basic model just including variables linked to wind-farm monitoring and turbine characteristics (Table 1). Indeed, these models (whose difference is the inclusion or not of turbine altitude) are 4.76 (model 1: 1/0.21) and 3.33 (model 2: 0.7/0.21) more likely, given the data, than the basic one (Table 1). The other models including different descriptors of vulture abundance (year-round aggregation of birds, distance to breeding colonies and/or roost sites) had less statistical support (Table 1). These results show how turbines located in areas with higher aggregations of the species (i.e., large breeding colonies) killed more birds than turbines located in less populated areas. Thus, although other non-evaluated factors are probably still affecting mortality at specific turbines, their location within the breeding vulture population is related to the number of bird deaths, even when controlling for time since wind-farm operation, for the existence of different intensities in search procedures (i.e., wind-farms with or without preventive vigilance) and for turbine characteristics (height and altitude above sea level). It should be noted that although more birds died during the non-breeding season, the main variable to describe this pattern is aggregation during the breeding period. Similarities in the aggregation pattern of the species during the breeding and the non-breeding seasons (large colonies remain as large communal roosts but small colonies disappeared; correlation between colony and roost site sizes: r = 0.70, 95% CI = 0.48– 0.83, n = 39) can explain this result.

## 3.2. Security distance: application to wind-farm planning

To guide managers in wind-farm planning, we modelled the relationship between the relative positions of turbines within the spatial distribution of the population of griffon vultures combined with data on mortality (obtained as presence/absence of death birds per turbine; error distribution: binomial, link function: logit) to obtain a setback distance for the installation of turbines. The best model included information on aggregation within breeding colonies, time since monitoring, existence of preventive vigilance protocols and season. The alternative model was similar, also including turbine altitude (DAIC = 0.21). The other models had less statistical support (DAIC > 2.01, Table 2). Expected probability of mortality could be thus presented against aggregation of breeding colonies (see Fig. 2 as an example using our local data), and managers can select from this plot the maximum year-round probability of mortality that they would assume when approving a windfarm placement. This value represents an objective criterion developed by taking information on the study area that could be applied during risk assessments.

Similar procedures could be applied to data gathered in other areas to adjust security placement to local variability in mortality. Moreover, this method can be also validated using species-specific information on mortality and aggregation of other species of interest. In the case of territorial species, distance to territories as well as aggregation (computed by using a modified version proposed by Carrete et al. (2006)) should be considered, as differences in social systems can change their relative importance as mortality predictors. As the limits imposed to wind-farm locations can be changed depending on the risk that could be assumed (which also depend on the species considered), this seems a straightforward and applicable criterion to be used in many different regions, situations and to a variety of species of conservation concern.

## 4. Discussion

The assumption that bird mortality at wind-farms is related to local bird abundances has been generally assumed as a positive relationship (Musters et al., 1996; Osborn et al., 2000; Drewitt and Langston, 2006; Kuvlesky et al., 2007; Tellería, 2009a, 2009b; Bright et al., 2008) but has been scarcely evaluated. Interestingly,

evaluation of this relationship has shown somewhat contradictory results (e.g., Barrios and Rodríguez, 2004; Everaert and Steinen, 2007; de Lucas et al., 2008). Here, we present tested support to the positive relationship between the relative abundance of griffon vultures, a species sensitive to collision at wind-farms (see below), and their mortality at wind-farm turbines. This finding contradicts previous results obtained in the same study area by de Lucas et al. (2008), but supports those of Barrios and Rodríguez (2004). The apparent lack of strength in this relationship between studies could be a consequence of sampling procedures. De Lucas et al. (2008), for example, based their main conclusion on two points, namely: (1) a lack of correlation between mortality rates obtained in a 9-year period and local (i.e., within wind-farms) bird abundances from only 1 year at two wind-farms, and (2) comparison between the abundance and mortality of griffon vultures recorded among seasons (n = 4). Conversely, Barrios and Rodríguez (2004), studying the same wind-farms but considering concurrent mortality rates and vulture abundances, found that more birds died when more birds were present at these developments. Moreover, their mortality rate increased during winter, the season during which bird flight behavior is riskier (i.e., higher ratio of birds observed within 5 m of the blades of operating turbines out of the total number of passes or observations within 250 m of the turbine lines; Barrios and Rodríguez, 2004). Overlooking inter-annual differences in local abundances of vultures and seasonal changes in bird flying behavior is a potentially serious problem that may affect for example avoidance behaviors (i.e., behaviors precluding risky situations such as flying in the vicinity of rotors; Chamberlain et al., 2006). In

the first case, changes in food abundance and distribution as well as in meteorological conditions can affect movements and, therefore, the number of birds flying at specific points from 1 year to the other (Martínez-Abraín et al., in press). In the second case, seasonal variations in bird flying behavior change the risk of collision of individuals throughout the year and are a major determinant of mortality rates (Barrios and Rodríguez, 2004; Garthe and Hüppop, 2004; Hoover and Morrison, 2005; Chamberlain et al., 2006). Thus, a coarser estimation of the abundance of individuals of a species potentially using the area (such as that used here) could be a better predictor of actual mortality than a finer but more punctual and local estimation subject to considerable observer, stochastic and systematic errors that affect its accuracy and precision (Chamberlain et al., 2006).

Regarding our previous comments, it seems that counting birds at specific points during particular periods of time has a very low predictive power when planning future developments. However, the use of other estimates of bird abundances such as the largescale spatial distribution of breeding colonies as well as their sizes could be more promising, mainly when dealing with species faithful to their territories, colonies or wintering areas such as many raptors. In these cases, even when birds can change their daily movements in response to local variability in resources (i.e. food) or conditions (i.e. wind), they must travel around their colonies or roost sites (Carrete and Donázar, 2005), and must face nearby turbines into which they may collide. Using this latter approach, we corroborated the positive relationship between bird distribution (location and size of bird aggregations), and mortality at wind-farm turbines, while offering a predictive tool useful in forecasting future impacts before the installation of new developments. Our results indicate that precise information on the distribution and abundance of sensitive species, such as large raptors, might be the best biological guideline to assess wind-farm location at a large scale (e.g., Tellería, 2009b; Bright et al., 2008). An interesting result is that aggregation of birds around turbines, but not their distance to breeding colonies, explain annual mortality. Thus, even when risk assessment considers distance to breeding colonies as a factor to evaluate the possibility of constructing a wind-farm, the combination between location and abundance of birds should be taken into account as a primary factor. Importantly, as our results indicate, the importance of aggregation of birds around turbines can be used to evaluate wind-farm locations in terms of the collision risk of susceptible species.

Previous studies have indicated a spatial overlap between windfarms and species of conservation concern (e.g., Fielding et al., 2006; Tellería, 2009a, 2009b; Carrete et al., 2009), while others have provided sensitivity maps based on bird distributions to guide wind-farm installation (e.g., Bright et al., 2008). These proposals are commonly viewed as risk maps where wind-farm impacts should be minimized. However, interpretations of these maps should not mistake interspecific differences in sensitivity to collision for conservation concern. The mortality database we are using shows how, compared to other raptor species, griffon vultures are particularly vulnerable to collision (Martínez-Abraín et al., in press). Thus, large regional abundances of this species can increase mortality rates to values as great as ca. 400 birds/year in areas such as Navarre (north Spain; Drewitt and Langston, 2006). In the other extreme, however, even very low values of additional mortality rates recorded at wind-farms can have negative demographic consequences on species of conservation concern (Martínez-Abraín et al., in press). Recently, Carrete et al. (2009) show how population sizes and therefore time to extinction of an endangered long-lived raptor, the Egyptian vulture Neophron percnopterus, strongly decreased when an additional wind-farm annual mortality rate of 0.015 and 0.008 for territorial and non-territorial birds, respectively, is included in population viability models. Thus, to assume

that collision mortality should increase with bird abundance because more birds are ‘available’ for collision may be too simplistic. Perhaps just as simplistic as to make interspecific generalizations about this relationship without taking into account specific sensitivities to collision at turbines. Hence, although landscape planning should include the spatial distribution and aggregation of sensitive species, other aspects such as conservation status (Garthe and Hüppop, 2004) should also be taken into account when selecting future wind-farm locations as well as when managing currently operating developments.

When a wind project is proposed in European countries, an environmental impact assessment is required by environmental authorities. These studies must include a section assessing the impact that the development is likely to have on the site’s bird populations (Environmental Impact Assessment Directive 97/11/EC). Environmental authorities use the overall assessment to reach a declaration on the environmental impact stating the significance and acceptability of the predicted effects. These declarations identify additional measures to mitigate and compensate potential negative environmental consequences and other conditions that should be met by the project developer such as the monitoring of the environmental impacts. If properly enforced, the environmental impacts hierarchy ‘‘avoid-minimize-compensate’’ would provide the regulated community with incentives to prevent wildlife and habitat impacts in sensitive areas and, if necessary, compensate for residual impacts through restoration or conservation projects (Cole, 2011). In Spain, wind-farm planning is competency of regional governments. In our case, the planning of wind-farm projects corresponds to the Andalusian government. Here, the project’s location is evaluated considering spatial environmental data available in the area (i.e., statutory protected areas, Important Bird Areas, nest sites, roost sites, rubbish dumps, pre-migratory settlement areas, eagle dispersal areas). A large amount of digitized data is available in Andalusia and rarely should a breeding site of an endangered bird species be overlooked in this phase of planning. Risk areas are established around breeding sites using a ‘‘risk radius’’ based on available data of species’ home ranges (Janss et al., 2010). However, risk radii have been arbitrary or based on old-fashioned data (Carrete et al., 2010). Consequently, observed mortality can be sometimes higher than that previously expected (Carrete et al., 2010). Monitoring program of environmental impacts imposed on approved projects are thus an important complement whose results should be used to implement corrective measures such as powering down or removing risky turbines and/or farms, and by placing them outside areas critical for endangered birds. It is relevant to consider that, for example, in our study area all vultures were killed by 214 out of 799 turbines (ca. 27%) and more than 50% of those deaths occurred in only two wind-farms. Nevertheless, the current framework is proving ineffective for planning, and the reality is that removing or reforming existing wind-farms is virtually impossible due to the absence of regulatory and flexible administrative mechanisms (only the activity of three wind-farms in Spain in Navarra, Castilla-León and Valencia have been paralyzed because of high mortality rates of birds).

Making decisions that affect biodiversity conservation has often to be made on the basis of incomplete information, ignorance about processes and speculations about outcomes. In this sense, it is important to anticipate and take action to avert potential, uncertain environmental harm. The precautionary principle is a widely and increasingly accepted general principle of environmental policy, law, and management (Cooney, 2004). In the windfarms-wildlife scenario, we reaffirm the need for applying the precautionary principle during wind-farm planning to minimize the impact of wind-farms on populations of long-lived species (Carrete et al., 2010).
